cues.text: A Peace Suddenly Broken
For nearly forty years after the death of the Emperor Valerian in 260, the Church enjoyed what Christian writers came to call the Peace of the Church .
This period of official toleration was so sustained that congregations built churches openly, and Christians rose to real prominence, even within the imperial household itself.

This long calm ended abruptly under Diocletian , whose junior co-emperor Galerius , a committed and determined enemy of the Christian faith, pressed his reluctant senior colleague toward a final, decisive confrontation with the growing Church.
Diocletian himself was, by most contemporary accounts, not naturally a cruel man.
For years, he resisted pressure to turn against a religion that, by the century's end, had penetrated every level of Roman society, including his own household staff.
Four Escalating Edicts
The persecution began on February 23, 303, with the demolition of the great cathedral at Nicomedia .
Within days, an edict ordered the destruction of churches and the burning of sacred Scriptures throughout the empire.
It also imposed the loss of civil rank on any Christian of honorable station who refused to recant.
Three further edicts over the following two years steadily widened the assault.
They ordered the imprisonment of bishops, priests, and deacons; their torture and compulsion to sacrifice by any means necessary.
Finally, in 304, they demanded universally that every inhabitant of the empire, Christian or not, offer sacrifice to the gods on pain of death.
The Fiercest Persecution the Church Had Known
Eusebius, an eyewitness to much of what followed, recorded extraordinary brutality across the eastern provinces where Galerius held sway.

Churches burned, sacred books were confiscated and destroyed by the cartload, and Christians of every age and station were tortured, mutilated, and executed in numbers no earlier persecution had approached.
These events prompted later chroniclers to remember the years simply as the Great Persecution .
Contemporary and near-contemporary accounts describe Christians of every station subjected to torture designed less to kill quickly than to break resolve.
These methods included the rack, fire, wild beasts, and forced labor in the mines, with entire congregations sometimes seized and executed together during a single Sunday assembly.
Uneven Enforcement Across a Divided Empire
The persecution's severity varied enormously depending on which of the empire's co-rulers governed a given province.
In the West, under the more moderate Constantius Chlorus, enforcement remained comparatively mild.

In the East, under Galerius and later his successor Maximinus Daia, the persecution continued to rage with undiminished ferocity for nearly a decade after Diocletian's own retirement from power in 305.
An Empire's Reluctant Surrender
By 311, even the dying Galerius, tormented by illness he could not help but read as divine judgment, issued an edict of toleration in his own name.
This formally admitted the persecution's failure to eradicate the Christian faith it had targeted with such determination.
The reversal became complete only a few years later, when Constantine, the new master of the West, extended full legal toleration to the Church in the Edict of Milan.
Legacy

Within barely a decade of its bloodiest edicts, the empire that had tried to burn every copy of Scripture and level every church to its foundations found itself ruled by its first openly Christian emperor.

This reversal was so complete and so swift that it remains, in the memory of the Church, the clearest possible demonstration that no persecution, however total its ambition, has ever succeeded in outlasting the faith it set out to destroy.
The Great Persecution stands as the final and fiercest trial of the Church's ancient age of martyrs, and, in its utter failure, the fitting close to that whole era of Roman hostility.
We recognize in this final and fiercest of the ancient persecutions a pattern the whole history of the Church would come to understand as strangely, almost predictably reliable.
Moments of greatest apparent danger to the faith have again and again preceded, rather than prevented, its most decisive and lasting triumphs.
